screens.title: Quality Attributes: How well a system works
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we shift focus from what a system does to how well it does it. Quality Attributes are measurable properties—like response time, security, and maintainability—that tell us whether a design will meet user expectations in real conditions. This matters because a system that implements features but is slow, insecure, or hard to change will fail in practice. You will learn to name common QAs, express them in measurable terms, and reason about the trade-offs architects face when improving one attribute affects another. For example, adding strong encryption improves security but can slow response time; we will see how to write SMART statements that make such trade-offs visible and testable. By the end of these slides you will be able to identify the top QAs for a system, describe relevant metrics, and start drafting measurable QA statements for design reviews. Consider now: which quality attribute would you prioritize for a payment system, and why?

screens.title: What are Quality Attributes?
screens.narratorSegment: Quality Attributes are the measurable properties of a software system that describe how it operates rather than what it does. Think of a car analogy: functional requirements say the car drives and has four wheels; quality attributes say the car gets 40 miles per gallon, reaches highway speeds safely, or is easy to repair. Formally, QAs describe operational characteristics like performance, availability, security, and maintainability. They guide architectural decisions: choosing a database, adding caches, or designing redundancy are responses to QA goals. A common misconception is treating QAs as optional polish. In reality they are requirements that must be specified, prioritized, and tested. For example, "process payments" is functional; "process payments within two seconds for 99% of transactions" is a performance QA that drives choices such as synchronous vs asynchronous processing and caching strategies. To work with QAs, you must make them measurable, choose metrics and tests, and accept that improving one attribute often affects others. Reflect: what quality attribute would change your design most if you increased its priority from medium to high? What are Quality Attributes? means qas are measurable system properties that directly shape architecture and deployment choices.. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and a concise working metaphor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: QAs are measurable system properties that directly shape architecture and deployment choices.

content.html:
Core Concept
What are Quality Attributes?
Measurable properties describing how well a system performs its functions. They direct architectural choices and validation activities.
Metaphor — the car
Functional: the car drives. QA: it is fuel-efficient, safe, and easy to repair. That how-well view shapes design decisions.
Common misconception
Thinking QAs are optional polish. They are requirements that must be prioritized and validated like any other requirement.
Examples
Functional → Non-functional
"Process payments" (functional) → "Process payments within 2 seconds for 99% of transactions" (performance QA).
Why it matters
A feature that works but is too slow or insecure will not satisfy users or business goals; QAs prevent that disconnect.
Check your understanding
Try converting a feature you know into one measurable QA using percentiles or uptime targets.
Key Takeaway

Quality attributes answer 'how well' and must be measurable so architects can validate designs.

screens.title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the distinction between functional and non-functional requirements is foundational. Functional requirements describe specific actions or behaviors—what the system must do. Examples include allowing a user to place an order or to upload a document. Non-functional requirements, or quality attributes, describe the qualities of those actions—how well they must be performed, under which constraints, and to what measurable standard. A helpful exercise is to take a user story and ask two follow-up questions: what must it do, and how well must it do it? For instance, a file upload feature is functional; its performance QA might be that files up to 50 megabytes upload within five seconds for 95% of attempts under expected network conditions. A common mistake is to leave the how-well part unspecified. That makes it impossible to choose technologies, set tests, or accept a delivery. In planning workshops, always convert vague adjectives like "fast" or "secure" into testable criteria and attach a metric and threshold. Which adjective have you seen left vague in a real project, and how would you make it SMART? Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements means functional requirements describe actions; non-functional requirements describe the qualities of those actions and must be measurable.. In practical terms, clear contrasts and examples you can use in requirements workshops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition
Functional Requirements
Describe specific behaviours or actions the system must perform. Captured as user stories or use cases.
Example
"The system shall allow users to upload documents."
Why it matters
Functional stories define scope and acceptance criteria for features.
Definition
Non-Functional Requirements (Quality Attributes)
Specify qualities, constraints, and measurable targets such as performance, availability, and security.
Example
"Files up to 50 MB shall upload within 5 seconds for 95% of attempts under expected network conditions."
Why it matters
Provides measurable targets that drive architecture, testing, and operational choices.
Quick practice
Pick a feature you know and write one functional sentence and one measurable QA sentence. This small habit avoids vague acceptance criteria and simplifies design trade-offs.

screens.title: Common Quality Attributes
screens.narratorSegment: Architects use a common vocabulary for quality attributes when evaluating designs. The most frequently encountered ones include performance, scalability, security, reliability, availability, maintainability, usability, portability, testability, and recoverability. Each attribute focuses on a different concern: performance measures speed and throughput; scalability captures the system's ability to grow under load; security protects data and access; reliability measures correct operation over time. Availability is the percentage of time the system meets users' needs, often achieved with redundancy. Maintainability describes how easily the system can be modified and tested. These attributes often overlap and interact. For instance, measures you take to improve availability, like data replication, can increase maintenance complexity. A practical approach is to list the candidate QAs for your project, rank them by business priority, and then translate the top priorities into SMART statements you can test. Which three of these attributes would you expect to prioritize for a high-traffic public website, and why? screens.title: Performance: Metrics and Examples
screens.narratorSegment: Performance is about speed and capacity: how quickly the system responds, how many requests it can handle, and how latency behaves under load. Good performance targets use percentiles and explicit load descriptions. For example, specify that login requests should complete within 500 milliseconds for 95% of requests under a load of 1,000 concurrent users. That statement says what to measure, the acceptable threshold, and the load context. To validate performance you use benchmarks and load testing tools that reproduce realistic traffic patterns and measure percentiles such as the 95th or 99th. Beware of two common mistakes: measuring only average response time, which hides long tails, and testing under unrealistic conditions that don't represent production. A simple process to specify and validate performance is: 1) choose the operation and realistic load, 2) pick percentile targets and thresholds, 3) design tests that reproduce expected traffic, and 4) run benchmarks and compare results. After testing, translate outcomes into design decisions like adding caching, batching requests, or switching to asynchronous patterns. Ask: what realistic load should you use for your next performance test? Performance: Metrics and Examples means use percentiles and realistic load profiles; avoid averages and unrealistic test conditions.. In practical terms, how to specify performance targets and validate them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use percentiles and realistic load profiles; avoid averages and unrealistic test conditions.

content.html:
Process Flow
Specifying Performance
1. Choose operation and load
Pick a user-visible operation and a realistic concurrent user profile.
2. Select percentiles and thresholds
Use p95, p99 rather than averages and specify thresholds under the chosen load.
3. Design and run tests
Create load tests that mirror production behavior and measure the selected percentiles.
4. Act on results
If tests fail, consider caching, batching, horizontal scaling, or asynchronous processing.
Concrete example
SMART performance statement
"Login requests shall complete within 500 milliseconds for 95% of requests under a sustained load of 1,000 concurrent users."
Common mistakes
  • Relying on average latency instead of percentiles.
  • Testing without realistic user behavior or data sizes.
Key Takeaway

Measure percentiles under realistic load, then use results to guide caching and scaling choices.

screens.title: Scalability: Horizontal vs Vertical Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Scalability is the system's ability to handle increased load by adding resources. Two common strategies are vertical scaling—adding more resources to a single machine—and horizontal scaling—adding more machines to distribute load. Vertical scaling can be simpler to implement but is limited by single-machine constraints and can be costly for very large capacity. Horizontal scaling offers better fault isolation and potentially unbounded capacity, but it requires careful design for statelessness, distributed data, and coordination. A common misconception is that horizontal scaling always solves performance problems; it only helps when the design supports distribution. For example, a stateless web service can scale horizontally behind a load balancer, but a tightly coupled stateful component may require redesign or sharding. Practical steps: classify components as stateful or stateless, choose partitioning strategies for data, and design for eventual consistency where appropriate. After deciding a direction, write a scalability QA such as "The system shall support a 50% traffic increase within 10 minutes by adding instances and without exceeding 2x latency." How would you partition data for that goal? Scalability: Horizontal vs Vertical Strategies means choose vertical scaling for simplicity and horizontal scaling for growth, but design components to support the chosen model.. In practical terms, when to scale up, when to scale out, and the trade-offs involved. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Scaling Strategies
Vertical Scaling
Increase CPU, RAM, or I/O on a single machine. Simple but limited and can increase single-point risk.
Horizontal Scaling
Add more machines and distribute load. Supports growth and fault isolation but requires distributed design.
Design considerations
Stateless services, data partitioning, coordination, and consistency models are key for horizontal scaling.
Concrete example
Scaling a document collaboration service
Stateless API servers can scale horizontally behind a load balancer; document storage may require sharding and replication to support large user bases.
Pitfall
Assuming you can horizontally scale without changing data models. If crucial state is centralized, performance will bottleneck.
Key Takeaway

Design components for the scaling pattern you plan to use; statelessness and partitioning make horizontal scaling feasible.

screens.title: Security as a Quality Attribute
screens.narratorSegment: Security is a broad quality attribute covering confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data and services. To turn security into a testable requirement, you must specify standards, controls, and verification steps. For example, rather than saying "the system shall be secure," state that sensitive data must use AES-256 encryption at rest and TLS 1.2 or higher in transit, and that the system will undergo annual penetration testing with no critical findings. This statement includes what protection is required and an audit mechanism. Architects must also plan for authentication and authorization, key management, and vulnerability management processes. A common misconception is that adding encryption everywhere solves security; encryption is necessary but not sufficient. You also need secure design, least privilege, monitoring, and incident response. When evaluating designs, ask whether each security QA has an associated verification plan such as audits, tests, or threat modeling. How would you phrase a SMART security statement for user access to confidential documents? Security as a Quality Attribute means specify concrete controls and verification steps—encryption standards, access controls, and audit plans—so security becomes testable.. In practical terms, specifying and validating security qas in architectures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Security Focus
Specifying Security QAs
Make security measurable by naming controls and audits. Encryption standards, access models, and required testing all belong in a SMART statement.
Example SMART statement
"All sensitive documents shall be encrypted at rest using AES-256, in transit using TLS 1.2+, and the system shall pass an annual penetration test with zero critical vulnerabilities."
Design elements
  • Authentication and authorization model (least privilege)
  • Key and secrets management
  • Vulnerability scanning and incident response
  • Logging and monitoring for suspicious activity
Common misconception
Assuming encryption alone is sufficient. Security requires layered controls and validation processes.
Key Takeaway

Spell out controls and audits so security can be validated, not assumed.

screens.title: Reliability vs Availability
screens.narratorSegment: Reliability and availability are closely related but address different concerns. Reliability measures the ability of a system to perform required functions under stated conditions for a period of time—often expressed with metrics like mean time between failures. Availability measures the percentage of time a system is operational and accessible to users. High availability is typically achieved with redundancy and fault-tolerant design. A system can be reliable yet unavailable during maintenance windows, so architects must plan maintenance strategies and failover to meet availability targets. For instance, specifying 99.99% availability drives replication, automated failover, and health checks. A typical mistake is equating availability with reliability or ignoring maintenance and recovery windows when calculating uptime. Practical steps include designing for graceful degradation, automated recovery, and clear recovery time objectives. Reflect: what replication or redundancy strategy would you choose to achieve four nines availability for a core service? narration.text: Reliability and availability are closely related but address different concerns. Reliability
Ability to perform required functions under stated conditions for a specified period. Measured by MTBF and error rates.

Automated testing, defensive coding, graceful error handling, and monitoring for early detection.
Definition

screens.title: Maintainability, Testability, and Portability
screens.narratorSegment: Maintainability, testability, and portability are attributes that reduce long-term cost and increase the pace of change. Maintainability focuses on how easily code can be understood and modified—factors include modularity, clear interfaces, and low cyclomatic complexity. Testability is about designing code and systems so that tests can be written and automated easily, which often means designing modular components and providing hooks for instrumentation. Portability refers to moving a system between environments or platforms with minimal effort—this influences choices around platform-specific APIs and dependencies. Together, these attributes determine how quickly teams can deliver features and fix defects. A misconception is to prioritize immediate performance improvements while ignoring maintainability; over time that choice slows feature delivery and increases risk. Practically, include coding standards, automated test coverage targets, and containerization strategies in QA statements; for example, require 80% unit test coverage for core modules and a documented container image life-cycle to support portability. How would you balance immediate delivery speed with maintainability on a tight schedule? screens.title: Writing SMART Quality Attributes
screens.narratorSegment: Vague statements like "the system should be fast" are not actionable. The SMART framework gives us a practical structure: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. A strong QA statement names the operation, the metric, the threshold, the context, and a verification method. For example, instead of saying "secure", specify that "sensitive customer data shall be encrypted at rest with AES-256 and in transit using TLS 1.2+, and the system shall pass an annual penetration test with no critical vulnerabilities." For performance, write statements that include percentiles and load context. To practice, follow four steps: 1) pick a top-priority QA, 2) choose a precise metric and percentile, 3) set a threshold and realistic load or condition, and 4) choose a verification method such as a benchmark or audit. A misconception is to set unattainable thresholds. Ensure the target is achievable given budget and technology, or mark it as a stretch goal. Write one SMART QA now for a feature you care about. Specification
SMART Quality Attributes
Specific
Name the operation or data the QA covers.
Measurable
Pick a metric like p95 latency, throughput, or uptime percentage.

screens.title: Architectural Trade-offs and Examples
screens.narratorSegment: Architectural trade-offs are the unavoidable compromises made when two quality attributes conflict. For example, strengthening security with additional encryption layers and synchronous authorization checks can degrade performance. Increasing availability through replication can raise operational cost and complexity, affecting maintainability. Architects must understand the project's priorities and make decisions that are good enough for the business context. A useful method is to list conflicting attributes, estimate their impact, and choose an architecture that satisfies higher-priority QAs while documenting acceptable degradation in lower-priority areas. Consider a banking system: prioritize security and reliability over ultra-low latency. Conversely, an online multiplayer game prioritizes low latency and scalability, accepting more frequent deployments and code churn. A common mistake is optimizing for too many QAs at once. Use evidence and SMART statements to validate trade-offs and communicate risk to stakeholders. Ask yourself: which QA trade-off would you accept to meet a strict budget constraint? Reasoning about Trade-offs
List priorities, estimate impacts, and choose designs that align with business goals. Use SMART QAs and tests to validate choices.
Banking example
Prioritize security and reliability even if it costs some latency. Design for strong encryption, audits, and replication.
Game example
Prioritize low latency and horizontal scaling; accept faster iteration and more operational complexity.
Decision checklist
  • Rank QAs by business priority.

  • Create SMART targets for the prioritized QAs.

screens.title: Measuring Quality Attributes and Using ATAM
screens.narratorSegment: Measuring quality attributes requires concrete metrics and repeatable tests. Use load testing, synthetic benchmarks, monitoring, security audits, and usability studies to collect data against your SMART QAs. For performance, measure percentiles under realistic traffic. For security, run penetration tests and track vulnerability severity. For availability, use uptime monitoring and incident logs. Architects also use structured evaluation methods like the Architectural Trade-off Analysis Method: ATAM helps identify how well an architecture satisfies multiple QAs and where risks and trade-offs live. ATAM sessions expose sensitivity points—changes that strongly affect certain attributes—and trade-off points—decisions that improve one attribute at the expense of another. The output is a prioritized list of risks and recommendations. A common error is to collect metrics without linking them back to requirements. Always tie measurement results to the QA statements they validate, and adapt architecture or operations when tests show gaps. Consider: what monitoring would you add to ensure your top QA remains satisfied in production? screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three core ideas in mind as you design systems. First, quality attributes are measurable statements about how a system operates; they are as important as functional requirements because they drive architecture and testing. Second, always make QAs SMART: name the metric, threshold, context, and verification method so teams can validate outcomes. Third, treat trade-offs explicitly: prioritize attributes by business importance, document acceptable degradations, and use measurements and structured evaluations like ATAM to support decisions. These rules will help you avoid vague requirements, reduce rework, and create architectures aligned with stakeholder priorities. As you leave this chapter, try converting one feature into a functional sentence and one SMART QA, then outline how you would test the QA in production. That small habit will improve design clarity and reduce late surprises.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we shift focus from what a system does to how well it does it. Quality Attributes are measurable properties—like response time, security, and maintainability—that tell us whether a design will meet user expectations in real conditions. This matters because a system that implements features but is slow, insecure, or hard to change will fail in practice. You will learn to name common QAs, express them in measurable terms, and reason about the trade-offs architects face when improving one attribute affects another. For example, adding strong encryption improves security but can slow response time; we will see how to write SMART statements that make such trade-offs visible and testable. By the end of these slides you will be able to identify the top QAs for a system, describe relevant metrics, and start drafting measurable QA statements for design reviews. Consider now: which quality attribute would you prioritize for a payment system, and why?

These objectives orient our study of quality attributes. First, you will define what a quality attribute is and explain why it matters for architecture. Second, you will be able to distinguish functional requirements—what the system does—from non-functional requirements—how well it does those things—and show their relationship with concrete examples. Third, you will identify common quality attributes such as performance, scalability, security, maintainability, availability, and reliability, and categorize them so you can prioritize design decisions. Fourth, you will practice specifying measurable QA statements using the SMART criteria and understand basic techniques for measuring and evaluating them. Each objective is designed to move you from recognition to applied skill: from naming attributes to writing measurable requirements and analyzing trade-offs. By the end, you should be able to take a system idea and propose at least five quality attributes with clear, testable statements that will guide architectural choices.

Beyond definitions, these objectives focus on application. You will learn to analyze how QAs influence design choices, for example picking replication and redundancy patterns to meet availability goals. You will practice writing performance and security QAs as concrete statements that can be tested with benchmarks and audits. You will also learn a basic method to evaluate trade-offs so you can explain why a design favors one quality over another. Finally, you will use measurement techniques—load testing, penetration testing, and uptime monitoring—to validate whether an architecture meets its stated QAs. Each activity trains a skill: analysis, specification, evaluation, and measurement. Practically, this means after the chapter you should be able to join an architecture review and argue for a trade-off with measurement-backed reasoning and a SMART QA to verify the result.

Quality Attributes are the measurable properties of a software system that describe how it operates rather than what it does. Think of a car analogy: functional requirements say the car drives and has four wheels; quality attributes say the car gets 40 miles per gallon, reaches highway speeds safely, or is easy to repair. Formally, QAs describe operational characteristics like performance, availability, security, and maintainability. They guide architectural decisions: choosing a database, adding caches, or designing redundancy are responses to QA goals. A common misconception is treating QAs as optional polish. In reality they are requirements that must be specified, prioritized, and tested. For example, "process payments" is functional; "process payments within two seconds for 99% of transactions" is a performance QA that drives choices such as synchronous vs asynchronous processing and caching strategies. To work with QAs, you must make them measurable, choose metrics and tests, and accept that improving one attribute often affects others. Reflect: what quality attribute would change your design most if you increased its priority from medium to high? What are Quality Attributes? means qas are measurable system properties that directly shape architecture and deployment choices.. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and a concise working metaphor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the distinction between functional and non-functional requirements is foundational. Functional requirements describe specific actions or behaviors—what the system must do. Examples include allowing a user to place an order or to upload a document. Non-functional requirements, or quality attributes, describe the qualities of those actions—how well they must be performed, under which constraints, and to what measurable standard. A helpful exercise is to take a user story and ask two follow-up questions: what must it do, and how well must it do it? For instance, a file upload feature is functional; its performance QA might be that files up to 50 megabytes upload within five seconds for 95% of attempts under expected network conditions. A common mistake is to leave the how-well part unspecified. That makes it impossible to choose technologies, set tests, or accept a delivery. In planning workshops, always convert vague adjectives like "fast" or "secure" into testable criteria and attach a metric and threshold. Which adjective have you seen left vague in a real project, and how would you make it SMART? Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements means functional requirements describe actions; non-functional requirements describe the qualities of those actions and must be measurable.. In practical terms, clear contrasts and examples you can use in requirements workshops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Architects use a common vocabulary for quality attributes when evaluating designs. The most frequently encountered ones include performance, scalability, security, reliability, availability, maintainability, usability, portability, testability, and recoverability. Each attribute focuses on a different concern: performance measures speed and throughput; scalability captures the system's ability to grow under load; security protects data and access; reliability measures correct operation over time. Availability is the percentage of time the system meets users' needs, often achieved with redundancy. Maintainability describes how easily the system can be modified and tested. These attributes often overlap and interact. For instance, measures you take to improve availability, like data replication, can increase maintenance complexity. A practical approach is to list the candidate QAs for your project, rank them by business priority, and then translate the top priorities into SMART statements you can test. Which three of these attributes would you expect to prioritize for a high-traffic public website, and why? Common Quality Attributes means a working list of qas helps architects prioritize trade-offs and convert priorities into testable requirements.. In practical terms, a practical catalog architects use every day. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Performance is about speed and capacity: how quickly the system responds, how many requests it can handle, and how latency behaves under load. Good performance targets use percentiles and explicit load descriptions. For example, specify that login requests should complete within 500 milliseconds for 95% of requests under a load of 1,000 concurrent users. That statement says what to measure, the acceptable threshold, and the load context. To validate performance you use benchmarks and load testing tools that reproduce realistic traffic patterns and measure percentiles such as the 95th or 99th. Beware of two common mistakes: measuring only average response time, which hides long tails, and testing under unrealistic conditions that don't represent production. A simple process to specify and validate performance is: 1) choose the operation and realistic load, 2) pick percentile targets and thresholds, 3) design tests that reproduce expected traffic, and 4) run benchmarks and compare results. After testing, translate outcomes into design decisions like adding caching, batching requests, or switching to asynchronous patterns. Ask: what realistic load should you use for your next performance test? Performance: Metrics and Examples means use percentiles and realistic load profiles; avoid averages and unrealistic test conditions.. In practical terms, how to specify performance targets and validate them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Scalability is the system's ability to handle increased load by adding resources. Two common strategies are vertical scaling—adding more resources to a single machine—and horizontal scaling—adding more machines to distribute load. Vertical scaling can be simpler to implement but is limited by single-machine constraints and can be costly for very large capacity. Horizontal scaling offers better fault isolation and potentially unbounded capacity, but it requires careful design for statelessness, distributed data, and coordination. A common misconception is that horizontal scaling always solves performance problems; it only helps when the design supports distribution. For example, a stateless web service can scale horizontally behind a load balancer, but a tightly coupled stateful component may require redesign or sharding. Practical steps: classify components as stateful or stateless, choose partitioning strategies for data, and design for eventual consistency where appropriate. After deciding a direction, write a scalability QA such as "The system shall support a 50% traffic increase within 10 minutes by adding instances and without exceeding 2x latency." How would you partition data for that goal? Scalability: Horizontal vs Vertical Strategies means choose vertical scaling for simplicity and horizontal scaling for growth, but design components to support the chosen model.. In practical terms, when to scale up, when to scale out, and the trade-offs involved. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Security is a broad quality attribute covering confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data and services. To turn security into a testable requirement, you must specify standards, controls, and verification steps. For example, rather than saying "the system shall be secure," state that sensitive data must use AES-256 encryption at rest and TLS 1.2 or higher in transit, and that the system will undergo annual penetration testing with no critical findings. This statement includes what protection is required and an audit mechanism. Architects must also plan for authentication and authorization, key management, and vulnerability management processes. A common misconception is that adding encryption everywhere solves security; encryption is necessary but not sufficient. You also need secure design, least privilege, monitoring, and incident response. Reliability and availability are closely related but address different concerns. Reliability measures the ability of a system to perform required functions under stated conditions for a period of time—often expressed with metrics like mean time between failures. Availability measures the percentage of time a system is operational and accessible to users. High availability is typically achieved with redundancy and fault-tolerant design. A system can be reliable yet unavailable during maintenance windows, so architects must plan maintenance strategies and failover to meet availability targets. For instance, specifying 99.99% availability drives replication, automated failover, and health checks. A typical mistake is equating availability with reliability or ignoring maintenance and recovery windows when calculating uptime. Practical steps include designing for graceful degradation, automated recovery, and clear recovery time objectives. Maintainability, testability, and portability are attributes that reduce long-term cost and increase the pace of change. Maintainability focuses on how easily code can be understood and modified—factors include modularity, clear interfaces, and low cyclomatic complexity. Testability is about designing code and systems so that tests can be written and automated easily, which often means designing modular components and providing hooks for instrumentation. Portability refers to moving a system between environments or platforms with minimal effort—this influences choices around platform-specific APIs and dependencies. Together, these attributes determine how quickly teams can deliver features and fix defects. A misconception is to prioritize immediate performance improvements while ignoring maintainability; over time that choice slows feature delivery and increases risk. Practically, include coding standards, automated test coverage targets, and containerization strategies in QA statements; for example, require 80% unit test coverage for core modules and a documented container image life-cycle to support portability. Vague statements like "the system should be fast" are not actionable. The SMART framework gives us a practical structure: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. A strong QA statement names the operation, the metric, the threshold, the context, and a verification method. Architectural trade-offs are the unavoidable compromises made when two quality attributes conflict. For example, strengthening security with additional encryption layers and synchronous authorization checks can degrade performance. Increasing availability through replication can raise operational cost and complexity, affecting maintainability. Architects must understand the project's priorities and make decisions that are good enough for the business context. A useful method is to list conflicting attributes, estimate their impact, and choose an architecture that satisfies higher-priority QAs while documenting acceptable degradation in lower-priority areas. Consider a banking system: prioritize security and reliability over ultra-low latency. Conversely, an online multiplayer game prioritizes low latency and scalability, accepting more frequent deployments and code churn. A common mistake is optimizing for too many QAs at once. Measuring quality attributes requires concrete metrics and repeatable tests. Use load testing, synthetic benchmarks, monitoring, security audits, and usability studies to collect data against your SMART QAs. For performance, measure percentiles under realistic traffic. For security, run penetration tests and track vulnerability severity. For availability, use uptime monitoring and incident logs. Keep three core ideas in mind as you design systems. First, quality attributes are measurable statements about how a system operates; they are as important as functional requirements because they drive architecture and testing. Second, always make QAs SMART: name the metric, threshold, context, and verification method so teams can validate outcomes. Third, treat trade-offs explicitly: prioritize attributes by business importance, document acceptable degradations, and use measurements and structured evaluations like ATAM to support decisions. These rules will help you avoid vague requirements, reduce rework, and create architectures aligned with stakeholder priorities.
